children: Shares of Mattel Inc. were falling after the maker of Barbie and Hot Wheels toys reported mixed quarterly earnings results and lowered its full-year guidance for sales and earnings. It also named a new chief operating officer.
Adjusted earnings of $1.30 a share beat the 94 cents a share Wall Street was expecting, but revenue of $1.81 billion was below the $1.84 billion expected.
Gross margin of 55% rose from 50% a year ago and beat the 51% analysts expected. But Mattel said that increase was primarily driven by $88 million in tariff refunds.
Shares fell 2.7% in late trading, after closing down 3.9% at $14.97 in regular Thursday trading. The stock is down 24.6% this year and down 19.8% over the past 12 months.
Mattel, which has faced pressure from activist shareholders, last month agreed to add Lee Matheson, a partner at EdgePoint Investment Group, Mattel's largest shareholder, to its board of directors.

Activists want the board to consider selling the company as it struggles financially, and those struggles have continued. Mattel lowered its guidance for full-year net sales growth to between 1% and 4%, down from the 3% to 6% growth it previously forecast. It lowered its adjusted operating income range to between $500 million and $570 million, from $580 million to $630 million previously.

Mattel now expects 2026 adjusted earnings $1.05 to $1.20 a share, down from the $1.27 and $1.39 it guided with second-quarter earnings. The guidance excludes the benefit from tariff refunds recognized so far this year, as well as any additional tariff refunds the company might receive before the end of 2026.
For the quarter, net sales increased 4% in North America and 5% internationally, and Hot Wheels continued performing well in the quarter.

Gross billings for dolls increased 4% to $703 million, primarily driven by partner brands, including KPop Demon Hunters, offset by a decline in Barbie. That's above the $673 million analysts expected.

Gross billings for vehicles grew 9% to $680 million, primarily because of Hot Wheels, and above the $672 million expected. Gross billings for Action Figures, Building Sets, Games, and Other rose 12% to $451 million, driven by Mattel163 and action figures, missing estimates for $498 million.
Gross billings for Infant, Toddler, and Preschool fell 16% to $221 million, because of a decline in Fisher Price, falling short of the $251 million expected.

"My first few weeks leading Mattel have reinforced my belief in the company's potential," Chairman and CEO Roger Lynch said. "I also see clearly where we must improve. We will focus our resources on our greatest opportunities and translate the strength of Mattel's portfolio and capabilities into more consistent financial performance."

Mattel also named Steve Totzke its president and Chief Operating Officer, effective Nov. 11, overseeing its global brand portfolio, sales, and commercial operations, and consumer products and experiences. Totzke, a 30-year Mattel veteran, was previously president and Chief Commercial Officer, overseeing global sales and commercial operations.
Roberto Stanichi, president and Chief Marketing and Brand Officer, is leaving to pursue another opportunity, effective Nov. 10.

Rival toy company Hasbro, maker of Play-Doh and Nerf, last month reported an earnings beat and a higher full-year outlook, saying that its bet on trading cards is paying off, with demand for Magic: The Gathering surging 34%.
